messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ama came to treatment at 20, already established in demanding work as a pharmacist, and spoke about the reason for coming in haltingly, as if language itself kept failing at the edge of what had happened to her. She was a young African woman living in the United States with her partner, outwardly composed and highly functional at work, but carrying a private sense that she had to stay on guard at all times. The traumatic event she referred to was a period of torture that she survived while others did not. When she tried to describe it, her account broke apart into fragments: a room, the force of being held down, the terror of being made to do things against her will, water used in a way that made her believe she might die. She could give pieces, but not a full story. She said she remembered only parts and that the rest seemed missing, and when she pushed herself to say more, she often stopped and shook her head, as though there were no words available for the worst moments.

What remained especially vivid was not a coherent narrative but an immediate physical knowledge. When memories came up, her body seemed to return before her mind did. She would stiffen, draw inward, and feel herself again in the same position she had been in during the torture, pinned by fear and bracing for what would come next. Water had become one of the most potent reminders. The sight of a flooded street after heavy rain, a wide river glimpsed from a car window, even water pooling in a parking lot could bring a jolt of dread that felt wildly out of proportion to the present but absolutely convincing in the moment. Arguments had a similar effect. Raised voices, sharp tones, the feeling that conflict was escalating could make her feel as though control was about to be taken from her. More than anything, being forced into something or even feeling pressured could bring a wave of panic and anger. What frightened her most was the sense of losing autonomy again.

In the months after the torture, Ama’s life became organized around preventing that feeling from returning. She had come to believe that if she let herself think directly about what happened, she would not be able to handle it. So she learned to turn away from anything that might bring it closer. She avoided times of day and situations that seemed to usher in nightmares, staying up later than she wanted or keeping herself occupied until she was exhausted. Sleep itself felt unsafe. At night she found it hard to fall asleep because she felt she needed to remain alert, listening for sounds in the apartment, noticing every shift in light or movement. During the day she constantly scanned her surroundings for signs of danger. She could not settle anywhere until she had identified how to get out. In restaurants, waiting rooms, and even at her pharmacy job, she checked exits almost automatically. When she started a shift, part of her attention went not only to medication orders and customer questions but to the door behind the counter, the stockroom passage, who was entering, and whether she could leave quickly if she had to.

That vigilance narrowed her world. She avoided people who resembled those involved in what had happened or whom she associated with them, sometimes leaving aisles in stores or asking a coworker to handle a customer because something about the person’s appearance made her body tense. Arguments with her partner were especially difficult. Even ordinary disagreements could feel dangerous once voices sharpened, and she might shut down, leave the room, or insist on ending the conversation immediately. To her, this was not overreacting; it felt necessary to prevent something catastrophic. Alongside this was a painful guilt she struggled to shake. She told herself she deserved to suffer because she had lived when others had not. At times this belief sat with her heavily and silently, less as a thought she examined than as a conclusion she felt she had no right to challenge.

By the time she sought help, the strain of living this way had become harder to contain. Her partner had noticed how little she slept and how often she seemed elsewhere even when she was physically present. At work, staying so alert to every entrance and every possible exit was exhausting, and she was increasingly aware that much of her day was spent bracing rather than resting. What finally brought her in was not a single crisis but the accumulation of too many moments in which water on the street, a customer’s angry tone, or the sensation of being cornered by someone else’s demands could pull her out of the present. She wanted help finding a way to live without feeling that danger was always one step away. At the same time, she was afraid that if she came too close to the memory, it would overwhelm her completely, and afraid as well of what it might mean to loosen the suffering she felt she owed.
